tldr: The authors propose a state-to-vision policy distillation framework that transfers knowledge from a privileged state-based teacher to an RGB-only student policy. Through theoretical and empirical analysis of distribution matching objectives between Gaussian policies, they achieve accurate and stable control on complex surgical manipulation tasks.
hero_caption: Overall framework: (a) First, a state-based teacher policy is trained via reinforcement learning (SAC) using privileged state information, such as precise object poses. (b) Then, with the teacher frozen while interacting with the environment, its action distribution is distilled into a student policy via distribution matching, using only RGB images and robot proprioceptive inputs.
overview:
Autonomous laparoscopic robotic manipulation requires millimeter-level precision for tasks like needle grasping and suturing. Reinforcement learning (RL) using ground-truth object coordinates (privileged states) available in simulators has been widely studied. However, reliably estimating the noiseless 3D positions of thin needles or soft organs in real surgical environments is exceptionally difficult. Vision-based RL, which directly maps camera images (RGB) to joint actions, avoids explicit state estimation pipelines, but surgical scenes present extreme visual sparsity: instruments and needles occupy only a few pixels across high-resolution frames. Consequently, training vision-based RL from scratch is prone to divergence and severe instability. Imitation learning (IL) offers stable supervised training, but collecting large volumes of high-quality expert demonstrations from surgeons is prohibitively expensive.

To bridge this gap, the authors turned to policy distillation: transferring knowledge from a privileged state-based teacher policy pre-trained in simulation to a vision-based student policy that takes only RGB images and the robot's proprioceptive joint information. Taking advantage of continuous Gaussian policies commonly used in continuous RL, they formulate distillation as distribution matching that can be evaluated analytically in closed form without Monte Carlo sampling.

Furthermore, they perform a rigorous mathematical comparison of gradient scaling and Hessian positive definiteness (local convexity regions) across five objectives: Forward KL (FKL), Reverse KL (RKL), Jeffreys Divergence (symmetric KL: JD), Wasserstein Distance (WD), and Mean Squared Error (MSE). In benchmarks on the surgical simulator SurRoL, their approach maintained roughly 70% success rates on challenging tasks like peg transfer and needle regrasping—where standard vision-based RL completely collapsed—and demonstrated that uncertainty-adaptive objectives such as JD and FKL offer superior robustness.
contributions: Formulated a continuous control policy distillation framework for surgical robots that transfers both the action mean and its uncertainty (variance) from a privileged state-based policy to an RGB-based vision policy.

Provided a unified first- and second-order gradient analysis of representative distribution matching objectives (FKL, RKL, JD, WD, MSE), theoretically proving differences in gradient scaling and the positive-definite (locally convex) regions of their Hessians.

Demonstrated on multiple laparoscopic tasks in the SurRoL benchmark that the proposed distillation achieves superior stability and around 70% success rates, outperforming pure vision-based RL and imitation learning.

sections.heading: How to train the eyes of a surgical robot? Distilling privileged knowledge into vision
sections.summary: State-based surgical policies that rely on ground-truth object coordinates fail in real environments, while learning purely from pixels diverges on dexterous tasks. To resolve this dilemma, this work proposes state-to-vision policy distillation for continuous control.
sections.details:
Core surgical gestures like needle insertion and tissue retraction require high dexterity, where sub-millimeter errors lead to surgical failure. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has advanced rapidly in surgical simulators, but most existing methods assume privileged state observations—exact positions and poses of objects provided directly by the simulation engine. In real surgery, however, real-time tracking of slender needles and deformable, translucent tissue is extraordinarily difficult.

Vision-based policies that map endoscopic RGB frames directly to control commands are promising alternatives. They eliminate hand-crafted state estimation pipelines and compound errors, yet they encounter severe visual sparsity. In high-resolution endoscopic frames, the relevant needle tip or tool tip occupies only a tiny fraction of pixels. Extracting meaningful features while exploring via pure RL is exceedingly difficult. On the other hand, imitation learning (IL) frames the problem as supervised learning, but gathering sufficient demonstrations from expert laparoscopic surgeons is drastically more expensive than in domestic manipulation tasks like folding clothes or opening bottles.

To overcome these limitations, the authors introduce a policy distillation framework. A privileged state-based policy trained in simulation acts as the "teacher," and an RGB-plus-proprioception (gripper state) "student" policy is trained to match the teacher's actions. While policy distillation historically focused on discrete action spaces like Atari, this paper targets continuous surgical control, treating distillation as distribution matching that aligns both the action mean and its uncertainty (variance).

sections.heading: At the crossroads: vision-based RL, surgical robotics, and policy distillation
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work in vision-based RL, surgical robotics, and policy distillation. Facing severe data scarcity and heavy computational overheads, distillation via closed-form continuous distribution matching emerges as an effective solution.
sections.details:
### Vision-based RL: Current status and limits
To train control policies directly from pixels, prior studies introduced Asymmetric Actor-Critic (using state-based critics), data-augmented algorithms like DrQ/DrQv2, and contrastive learning methods such as CURL. When abundant demonstrations exist, imitation learning frameworks like ALOHA have also shown remarkable progress. However, while these methods excel in humanoid locomotion or general table-top manipulation, they struggle in surgical robotics due to extreme precision requirements, visual sparsity, and the high cost of collecting surgical demonstrations.

### Learning-based surgical manipulation
Most surgical robotics research has focused on privileged state-based controllers. Deploying them into the real world requires a two-stage approach: running a vision perception pipeline to estimate poses and feeding those coordinates to the policy. Any perception error can trigger critical task failures. While some recent studies explored end-to-end vision-based control, they often rely on auxiliary depth information, segmentation masks, or computationally intensive pre-trained visual foundation models, leaving lightweight end-to-end learning largely unresolved.

### The promise of policy distillation
Policy distillation was originally developed to compress multi-task policies into a single network and was later adapted for robot skill transfer. Because it relies on supervised matching, its optimization is far smoother than pure RL, and it does not require collecting human expert demonstrations. However, most prior studies focused on discrete actions. How to select the right objective function to match continuous action distributions in high-precision surgical manipulation remained an open question.

Collecting transitions with the finalized teacher avoids using $\mathfrak{B}_1$, which contains sub-optimal transitions from early training stages, ensuring stable supervision.

sections.heading: What does matching distributions mean? Gradients and curvature of Gaussian policies
sections.summary: Formulating distillation as closed-form distribution matching between Soft Actor-Critic Gaussian policies, the authors derive first- and second-order gradients for FKL, RKL, JD, WD, and MSE. They mathematically prove that Jeffreys Divergence (JD) offers a broader convex optimization region alongside uncertainty adaptiveness.
sections.details:
### Gaussian policies and closed-form distribution matching
The paper defines a teacher policy $\pi_t = \mathcal{N}(\mu_t, \sigma_t^2)$ conditioned on privileged state $o_t$, and a student policy $\pi_s = \mathcal{N}(\mu_s, \sigma_s^2)$ conditioned on RGB frames and proprioception $o_s$. In continuous Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), policies are parameterized as independent multivariate Gaussians. Thanks to this parametric formulation, divergences and distances between the two distributions can be computed analytically in closed form without relying on Monte Carlo sampling.

### Five objective functions examined
The authors analyzed five representative objectives:
- **Forward KL (FKL)**: $\text{KL}(\pi_t \parallel \pi_s)$, characterized by a "mode-covering" behavior.
- **Reverse KL (RKL)**: $\text{KL}(\pi_s \parallel \pi_t)$, characterized by a "mode-seeking" behavior, tending to underestimate variance.
- **Jeffreys Divergence (JD)**: The symmetric KL divergence (SKL), defined as the sum of FKL and RKL, balancing both properties.
- **Wasserstein Distance (WD)**: The geometric distance derived from optimal transport (2-Wasserstein distance).
- **Mean Squared Error (MSE)**: Standard regression loss minimizing only the squared difference between action means $\mu$.

### First-order gradients and uncertainty adaptiveness
Inspecting the gradient with respect to the student's mean $\frac{\partial D}{\partial \mu_s}$ reveals crucial mechanistic differences:
- **WD and MSE**: Gradients are proportional solely to $\mu_s - \mu_t$, completely independent of variances $\sigma_t$ and $\sigma_s$. They apply uniform update magnitudes regardless of how confident the teacher is in a given action dimension.
- **FKL, RKL, and JD**: Gradients are adaptively scaled by variance terms. Dimensions with smaller variance (higher confidence) automatically receive larger gradient updates. FKL scales by student variance $\sigma_s^{-2}$, RKL scales by teacher variance $\sigma_t^{-2}$, and JD scales by both ($\sigma_t^{-2} + \sigma_s^{-2}$).

### Second-order gradients (Hessian) and convex regions (Proposition 1)
To examine optimization landscape stability, the authors analyzed the Hessian matrices with respect to the student's parameters $(\mu_s, \sigma_s)$. For RKL, WD, and MSE, the Hessians are positive definite everywhere (locally strongly convex), and cross-terms between $\mu_s$ and $\sigma_s$ are zero (decoupled). In fact, RKL reduces to an MSE loss weighted by teacher precision $\sigma_t^{-2}$.

In contrast, FKL and JD can have indefinite (non-convex) Hessians depending on parameter values. However, the authors proved that **the parameter region where the Hessian of JD is positive definite strictly contains that of FKL ($\mathcal{P}_{\text{FKL}} \subset \mathcal{P}_{\text{JD}}$)** (Proposition 1). Thus, JD not only prevents distributional bias by combining FKL and RKL, but also guarantees a significantly wider convex optimization basin than FKL, providing strong mathematical justification for its training stability.

sections.heading: Empirical results on complex surgical tasks: Distillation succeeds where pure RL collapses
sections.summary: Evaluated across five tasks in the SurRoL simulator, pure vision-based RL algorithms like DrQv2 collapsed to near 0% success on peg transfer and needle regrasping, while the proposed distillation (especially JD) maintained around 70% success. Feature map visualizations show the student accurately focuses on tool tips and target objects.
sections.details:
### Experimental setup and tasks
Experiments were conducted in the da Vinci-modeled surgical simulator "SurRoL" across five tasks of increasing difficulty:
- **NeedleReach**: A basic reaching task moving the tool tip to a target point.
- **GauzeRetrieve**: Grasping gauze and dragging it to a target destination.
- **NeedlePick**: Picking up a slender needle resting on a base.
- **PegTransfer**: Lifting a small block off a peg and transferring it onto another peg.
- **NeedleRegrasp**: The most challenging task, transferring a needle from one instrument to another in mid-air.

The teacher policy uses a 3-layer MLP taking ground-truth poses, while the student policy uses a lightweight 3-layer CNN followed by 3 fully connected layers, receiving RGB images from an endoscopic camera (ECM) alongside gripper coordinates.

### Main benchmark findings
Pure vision-based RL methods (CURL and DrQv2) achieved decent success on simple NeedleReach, but their performance dropped sharply on NeedlePick and collapsed to near 0% on dexterous tasks like PegTransfer and NeedleRegrasp. Imitation learning (ALOHA) performed well on NeedleReach (100%) and NeedlePick (81.2%), but deteriorated noticeably on PegTransfer (49.2%) and NeedleRegrasp (16.6%).

In contrast, the proposed policy distillation maintained consistent performance across all tasks, achieving roughly 70% success on both PegTransfer and NeedleRegrasp. This confirms distillation's ability to sidestep both the training instability of vision RL and the heavy demonstration dependence of imitation learning.

### Comparing distillation objectives: Alignment with theory
Comparing the loss functions revealed distinct behaviors that match theoretical predictions:
- **RKL instability**: On NeedlePick, RKL dropped sharply to a 39.8% success rate. The teacher policy had a very small standard deviation (around 0.3), causing RKL's gradient scale factor ($\sigma_t^{-2} \approx 11$) to excessively amplify updates, leading to unstable oscillations.
- **Benefit of uncertainty adaptiveness**: On PegTransfer and NeedleRegrasp, FKL and JD significantly outperformed MSE and WD, which ignore variance information.
- **JD superiority**: Across all benchmarks, JD consistently matched or outperformed FKL. This directly supports Proposition 1: JD's wider convex region yields more stable optimization in practice.

### What does the CNN look at? Feature map visualization
Visualizing the feature maps of the student's final convolutional layer (Figure F3) showed that the network did not rely on absolute coordinate artifacts. Instead, activation peaks consistently tracked the gripper tips and target objects (needle or gauze). Even a lightweight 3-layer CNN successfully captured the essential spatial relationships required for surgical manipulation.

captions.F3: Feature maps extracted from the student network's final convolutional layer across: (a) GauzeRetrieve, (b) NeedlePick, (c) PegTransfer, and (d) NeedleRegrasp. Strong activations (red and yellow regions) consistently track the robot's gripper and target object locations.

takeaways: When tasks require millimeter-level dexterity and targets are tiny in pixel space, training a privileged state-based teacher first and distilling it into a vision student is far more effective than training vision-based RL from scratch.

In continuous Gaussian policy distillation, closed-form distribution matching that accounts for action variance (uncertainty) outperforms standard MSE regression on action means in difficult manipulation tasks.

Jeffreys Divergence (symmetric KL) mathematically possesses a strictly larger positive-definite (convex) parameter region than Forward KL, delivering the most stable training while leveraging uncertainty adaptiveness.
Without relying on massive models or attention mechanisms, a lightweight 3-layer CNN can capture task-relevant surgical features when guided by an appropriate distillation objective.
limitations: Experiments are restricted to the SurRoL simulation environment; real-world sim-to-real transfer on physical hardware via domain randomization has not yet been demonstrated.
The framework relies entirely on teacher-driven rollouts for distillation, lacking student-driven exploration, self-improvement, or online adaptation to novel environmental shifts.
Gaussian policy outputs assume conditional independence across action dimensions (diagonal covariance matrix), omitting joint-to-joint correlation modeling.
